Notes:
1. Consolidated financial statements are prepared in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (“IFRS”).
2. Figures presented are rounded down to the nearest million yen.
3. Upon the adoption of IFRS, the Ajinomoto Group has introduced “Business profit” as a new profit level that will better enable
    investors, the Board of Directors, and the Executive Committee to grasp the core business results and future outlook of each
    business while also facilitating continual evaluation of the Group’s business portfolio by the Board of Directors and the Executive
    Committee. “Business profit” is defined as sales and share of profit of associates and joint ventures minus cost of sales, selling
    expenses, research and development expenses, and general and administrative expenses. Business profit does not include other
    operating income or other operating expenses.
4. In the 147th Fiscal Year, the Company finalized the provisional accounting treatment for a business combination, and the finalized
    figures have been reflected in the 146th Fiscal Year.
5. With a 2-for-1 stock split of the Company’s ordinary shares effective April 1, 2025, equity per share (attributable to owners of the
    parent company), basic earnings per share and diluted earnings per share were calculated based on the assumption that the stock
    split was conducted at the beginning of the 143rd Fiscal Year.

                                                                  -2-
2. History
   Month/Year                                                     Overview
May 1907         Established Suzuki Pharmaceutical GSK.
July 1908        Dr. Kikunae Ikeda obtained a patent for the production method of seasoning (monosodium glutamate). In
                 September of the same year, Saburosuke Suzuki II undertook the commercialization.
May 1909         Launched umami seasoning AJI-NO-MOTO®.
April 1912       Suzuki Pharmaceutical GSK. succeeded to the AJI-NO-MOTO® business, operated as a personal business of
                 Suzuki, and changed the company name to Suzuki Shoten GSK. at the same time.
September 1914   Completed the Kawasaki factory and started operation.
June 1917        Established S. Suzuki & Co. Ltd. and transferred all business of Suzuki Shoten GSK. to the said company,
                 and changed the business purpose of Suzuki Shoten GSK. to the acquisition and sale of securities and real
                 estates.
December 1925    Established S. Suzuki Co., Ltd. and transferred all business of Suzuki Shoten GSK. and S. Suzuki & Co.,
                 Ltd. to the said company, and dissolved these two companies. (present Ajinomoto Co., Inc.)
October 1932     Changed its company name to Ajinomoto Honpo S. Suzuki & Co., Ltd.
March 1935       Established Takara Oil Refining Co., Ltd. and started fat and oil business.
December 1940    Changed its company name to Suzuki Shokuryo Kogyo Co.
May 1943         Changed its company name to Dai-Nippon Chemical Co.
December 1943    Established the Saga factory in Saga prefecture. (present Kyushu Plant)
May 1944         Merged Takara Oil Refining Co., Ltd.
February 1946    Changed its company name to Ajinomoto Co., Inc.
May 1949         Listed on the stock market.
January 1956     Launched essential amino acids (for infusion) and started amino acid business.
July 1956        Established Ajinomoto Co. of New York, Inc. (present Ajinomoto Health & Nutrition North America, Inc.)
December 1956    Set up a central research laboratory in Kanagawa prefecture.
May 1958         Established Union Chemicals Inc. (present AJINOMOTO PHILIPPINES CORPORATION)
April 1960       Established Ajinomoto Co., (Thailand) Ltd.
March 1961       Set up a Yokkaichi factory in Mie prefecture. (present Tokai Plant)
July 1961        Established Ajinomoto (Malaya) Co., Ltd. (present Ajinomoto (Malaysia) Berhad)
March 1963       Entered into partnership with U.S.’s Corn Products International. (present Conopco, Inc.) (founded a joint-
                 venture company, Knorr Foods Co., Ltd.)
October 1967     Set up Specialty Chemicals Department and fully started specialty chemicals business.
February 1968    Established Ajinomoto del Perú S.A.
July 1969        Established PT Ajinomoto Indonesia.
November 1970    Launched HON-DASHI®.
December 1970    Established Ajinomoto Restaurant Foods Co., Inc. (present Ajinomoto Frozen Foods Co., Inc.) and started
                 frozen food business.
August 1973      Entered into partnership with U.S.’s General Foods Corporation. (founded a joint-venture company, present
                 Ajinomoto AGF, Inc.)
December 1974    Established Ajinomoto Interamericana Indústria e Comércio Ltda. (present Ajinomoto do Brasil Indústria e
                 Comércio de Alimentos Ltda.)
September 1981   Launched ELENTAL® and started pharmaceutical business.
May 1982         Launched export of aspartame and started sweeteners business.
June 1987        Made Knorr Foods Co., Ltd. a subsidiary.
September 1989   Acquired all shares of a Belgian chemical company S.A. OmniChem N.V. (present S.A. Ajinomoto
                 OmniChem N.V.)
December 1996    Established Ajinomoto (China) Co., Ltd.
October 2000     Spun off the frozen food business into a separate company and integrated it into Ajinomoto Frozen Foods
                 Co., Inc.
April 2001       Spun off the fat and oil business into a separate company and integrated it into Ajinomoto Oil Mills Co., Inc.
                 (present J-Oil Mills, Inc.)
February 2003    Ajinomoto Frozen Foods Co., Inc. acquired all shares of Frec Co., Ltd. from Nippon Sanso Ltd., and merged
                 with Frec Co., Ltd. in April 2003.
July 2003        Acquired all shares of ORSAN SA (present Ajinomoto Foods Europe S.A.S.), an umami seasoning
                 production and sales company held by Amylum France S.A.S.
February 2007    Acquired part of shares of Yamaki Co., Ltd. and entered into a capital and business alliance.
November 2011    Transferred operation of feed-use amino acid business to Ajinomoto Animal Nutrition Group, Inc.
                 (established in September 2011)


                                                           -3-
   Month/Year                                                   Overview
November 2014   Ajinomoto North America, Inc. acquired all equity interest of Windsor Quality Holdings, LP, a frozen food
                manufacturing and sales company in the U.S.
April 2015      Ajinomoto Frozen Foods U.S.A., Inc. merged Windsor Quality Holdings, LP and changed its company name
                to Ajinomoto Windsor, Inc. (present Ajinomoto Foods North America, Inc.)
April 2015      Made Ajinomoto General Foods, Inc. (present Ajinomoto AGF, Inc.) a subsidiary.
April 2016      AJINOMOTO PHARMACEUTICALS CO., LTD., engaged in the pharmaceutical business, succeeded a
                part of the business in the area of digestive diseases of Eisai Co., Ltd. through an absorption-type company
                split, became an affiliate accounted for by the equity method of the Company and changed the company
                name to EA Pharma Co., Ltd.
November 2016   Acquired 33.33% shares of Promasidor Holdings Limited, a major processed foods manufacturer that
                conducts business in countries in Africa and made it an affiliate accounted for by the equity method of the
                Company.
April 2019      Concentrated and reorganized the production system of part of the Kawasaki factory and Tokai Plant and
                Ajinomoto Packaging Co., Inc. to Knorr Foods Co., Ltd. and changed its company name to Ajinomoto Food
                Manufacturing Co., Ltd.
July 2021       Merged Ajinomoto Animal Nutrition Group, Inc.
December 2023   Ajinomoto North America, Inc. acquired all equity interest of Forge Biologics Holdings, LLC (present Forge
                Biologics, Inc.), a US-based gene therapy CDMO.




                                                         -4-
3. Description of business
 The Ajinomoto Group consists of Ajinomoto Co., Inc., 108 consolidated subsidiaries, and 15 affiliates accounted
 for by the equity method, and is engaged in areas of Sauce and Seasonings, Quick Nourishment, Solutions and
 Ingredients, Frozen Foods, Amino Acids for Pharmaceuticals and Foods, Bio-Pharma Services (CDMO services),
 Functional Materials (electronic materials and others), as well as other business activities.
 The position of the said Group’s business is as follows. (Companies marked with asterisks (*) are affiliates
 accounted for by the equity method.)

<Rate of Female Managers in the Group as a Whole>
The rate of female managers in the Group as a whole is 27%, and of Ajinomoto Co., Inc. is 14%. The Company
will continue to develop the basis and take initiatives toward women’s active participation in the Group as a
whole and aim for the rate of female managers group-wide to be 40% and of Ajinomoto Co., Inc. to be 30%.

<Gender wage gap in Ajinomoto Co., Inc.>
The integrated personnel system in Ajinomoto Co., Inc. sets the same gender wage range for the same level of
duties. However, the wages differ by gender due to the following factors.
The wage level by gender for full-time workers in non-management positions is almost the same in their 20s.
However, a wage gap according to job rank is approximately 88% for those in their 30s, as employees are
affected by limited work relocations, leaves, shorter working hours, and limited overtime work from life events
such as marriage, childbirth, and childcare. For workers in management positions, the gender wage gap of 95.5%
and 97.8% exists in the junior/mid-level and senior management positions, respectively, with the gap narrowing
as the position gets higher. Yet, the gender wage gap for full-time workers as a whole comes to 72.5% as the rate
of female employees in management positions with high pay levels is low. Female employees in their 20s
account for 41% of full-time workers compared to all female employees, accounting for 30% of full-time
workers, which indicates an increasing trend. In addition, Ajinomoto Co., Inc. aims to raise the rate of female
managers to 30% by FY2030 and is promoting measures to support the development of women, such as
AjiPanna Academy, to create a pipeline of human resources among managers. In the FY2024 career workshop of
AjiPanna Academy, all of 25 participants expressed their intention to challenge for higher positions.
Furthermore, in an engagement survey question (“If approached to take a higher position, I would like to accept
the offer.”), more than half of the women showed their intention of taking a higher position. We believe that the
number of female managers will increase, and the wage gap will gradually narrow in the future.
The wage gap in non-full-time workers is mainly due to the difference in the male-to-female ratio in the senior
rehired employees whose wages are higher than part-time employees. Considering the future decline in the
working population in Japan, the Company believes the wage gap will also gradually narrow for the non-full-
time workers by encouraging further active participation of women, whether working regularly or not, such as by
promoting the rehiring of senior women.




                                                     - 16 -
II.          Overview of Business
1. Management policy, business environment, issues to address
      The management policy, business environment, and issues to address of the Ajinomoto Group are as follows.
      Note that matters related to future developments that are mentioned in this section are judgments of the
      Ajinomoto Group that were made as of the end of the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025 (on a consolidated
      basis).


      <Entering the third year of our Medium-Term ASV Initiatives 2030 Roadmap>
      We are now in the third year since we announced our “Medium-Term ASV Initiatives 2030 Roadmap” (in
      February 2023), which outlines our vision for 2030 and the path to achieving it through backcasting*1. In
      implementing the roadmap, we abolished the more conventional three-year medium-term management plan that
      we had in place and instead endeavored to establish a series of “challenging targets set by management” (ASV
      Indicators*2), based on our long-term vision. To achieve these targets, the entire Ajinomoto Group is united in
      continuing to strive to create new value and transform our business model beyond organizational boundaries.
      *1 Backcasting is a method of envisioning how to achieve a goal by “working backward” from a desirable future to the present as
         a means of determining what one should do now.
      *2 Indices that encourage further growth and aspiration, consisting of economic indicators that demonstrate the degree to which
         the Ajinomoto Group’s business has performed financially, as well as social value indicators that are intended to measure the
         value that the Group strives to create on a societal level.




                                                                 - 17 -
<Improving our ability to put Our Philosophy into practice>
To realize the Ajinomoto Group’s Purpose, “Contributing to the well-being of all human beings, our society and
our planet with ‘AminoScience,’” we are refining our corporate strategy, as well as our business and functional
strategies, based on the ASV concept and the Ajinomoto Group Way (AGW), Ajinomoto Group’s code of
conduct. The “My Purpose Workshop,” a program initiated by Ajinomoto Group’s executive officers to deepen
its employees’ personal understandings of the Ajinomoto Group’s aspirations, is also being rolled out across the
entire group. By identifying certain points of overlap between each individual’s motivations and those of the
Ajinomoto Group, translating them into specific, relatable goals and encouraging them to take on certain
challenges while empathizing with others, we hope to further improve engagement*3 and enhance the Group’s
ability to put Our Philosophy into practice. We are now in the third year of the Medium-Term ASV Initiatives
2030 Roadmap, a stage that calls for greater strengthening of our conceptual and executive capabilities. As such,
we will strive to further develop our intangible assets – our people, technology, customers, and organization –
that are the source of our value creation, as well as the corporate culture that supports them.
*3 Deepening employees’ attachment to the Company and their work, as well as their willingness to contribute.


      <Our Philosophy>




<Contributing to the well-being of all human beings, our society and our planet with “AminoScience”>
The Ajinomoto Group aims to contribute to the well-being of all human beings, our society and our planet with
“AminoScience.” To this end, we believe it is necessary to reduce our environmental impact by 50% while also
extending the healthy life expectancy of 1 billion people by 2030.

<ASV management evolution scenario>
Under the new structure introduced in February 2025, we aim to further develop our ASV management
capabilities. Based on the Ajinomoto Group’s Purpose and the Ajinomoto Group Way (AGW), which serves as a
code of conduct, we will apply our “High-speed Development System”*4 to both speed up and scale up, creating
new businesses and transforming existing business models by forecasting*5 from the perspective of our present
business activities and backcasting from the perspective of our desired future state, thereby driving organic
growth and achieving an evolution of our business portfolio. Furthermore, while maintaining a corporate culture
that supports innovation, we will further advance our ASV management capabilities by further developing our
business management cycle and strengthening our intangible assets.

2. Disclosure of sustainability-related financial information
   <Our approach to sustainability>
   The Purpose of the Ajinomoto Group is to contribute to the well-being of all human beings, our society and our
   planet with “AminoScience.” We position sustainability at the core of ASV management. We advance specific
   initiatives under the Medium-Term ASV Initiatives 2030 Roadmap. These efforts align with the Six Material
   Themes identified as important issues (materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group.
   Our business depends on sound agrifood systems that produces and consumes food resources, and on the rich
   global environment that supports this system. This system both faces environmental changes and contributes
   significantly to the loss of natural capital. Adapting to these changes and restoring nature are urgent priorities
   for society and for the sustainable growth of our business as the global environment nears its limits. To this end,
   we advance efforts in climate change, biodiversity, and the circular economy. We also implement various
   initiatives to help achieve better nutritional balance, greater emotional well-being through food, and progress in
   both treatment and prevention.
   The Ajinomoto Group not only works to steadily reduce negative impacts through business activities but also
   aims to create stronger positive impacts across the value chain by leveraging our strengths in “AminoScience”
   and working with diverse stakeholders. Therefore, we strive for the sustainable enhancement of corporate value
   while implementing consistent efforts toward creating a healthy and prosperous society and healthier and more
   abundant lifestyles.




                                                        - 21 -
(1) Governance
    In the Ajinomoto Group, we honestly comply with the Ajinomoto Group Policies (AGP) that show the
    ideal way of thinking and action that the Group companies and their officers and employees should
    comply with, continue to develop and properly operate our internal control system, strengthen our system
    that considers sustainability as a framework active risk-taking system, and continuously enhance our
    corporate value. For the reflection of sustainability-related metrics in remuneration policy, please see “4.
    Status of corporate governance, etc., (4) Compensations for officers.”
    We are strengthening our sustainability promotion system to continuously increase our corporate value
    from the perspective of sustainability. As of the filing date of this document, this system is as outlined
    below.

    Framework for ESG and sustainability




    The Board of Directors has established the Sustainability Advisory Council, creating a system to provide
    recommendations about the Group’s approach to sustainability and ESG. It determines important issues
    (materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group that serve as guidelines for ASV management and supervises the
    execution of initiatives related to sustainability.
    The Executive Committee has established the Sustainability Committee and the Risk Management
    Committee as subordinate bodies and selects and extracts risks and opportunities based on important
    issues (materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group, assessing the degree of impact, formulating measures, and
    managing progress. In FY2024, the Executive Committee received two activity reports each from the
    Sustainability Committee and the Risk Management Committee.
    The Sustainability Advisory Council makes recommendations to enhance the corporate value of the
    Ajinomoto Group from the viewpoint of sustainability as a subordinate body of the Board of Directors.
    The Second Term Sustainability Advisory Council began in April 2023 and consists of four external
    experts, including investors and well-being specialists. An external expert also serves as council chair.
    The council meets at least twice a year to assess the efforts of the Board of Directors in the areas of
    materiality implementation, communication on implementation and information disclosure, and
    partnership building with stakeholders. The council submitted their final report to the Board of Directors
    in March 2025.
    The Sustainability Committee works with the Risk Management Committee to select and identify risks
    and opportunities based on materiality as well as assess their impact on the Ajinomoto Group, making
    proposals to the Executive Committee. The Sustainability Committee then explores and formulates
    countermeasures for sustainability risks and opportunities and manages their progress. In addition, the

                                                   - 22 -
    Sustainability Committee formulates the entire Ajinomoto Group’s sustainability strategy, promotes
    action themes (nutrition, environment, and society) based on this strategy, makes proposals and provides
    support for business plans from a sustainability viewpoint, and compiles internal information on ESG.
    The Risk Management Committee works with the Sustainability Committee to select and identify risks
    and opportunities based on materiality as well as assess their impact on the Ajinomoto Group, making
    proposals to the Executive Committee. The Risk Management Committee also develops and manages the
    progress of risk management measures to establish a strong corporate structure that ensures prompt and
    accurate responses to risks and crises, particularly with regard to risks that management should address
    (i.e., geopolitical risks, information security risks).

(2) Strategy
    The year 2024 was the hottest on record, with average temperatures rising by more than 1.5°C compared
    to pre-industrial revolution levels. It is our duty to ensure that the next generation can inherit a flourishing
    global environment and healthy society, which are essential to the sustainability of our business activities.
    Stabilizing the climate is a particularly urgent issue. To do so, we must become nature positive ‒ that is,
    stop the loss of nature and put nature on the road to recovery. We must also simultaneously address other
    mutually connected issues, such as circular economy, nutritionally balanced diets, and human rights.
    The Ajinomoto Group procures around 70% of its materials from the agricultural, livestock, and fishery
    industries, and therefore is highly dependent on the agrifood system, which itself is supported by the
    bounty of nature, or in other words, ecosystem services. The agrifood system accounts for more than 20%
    of all GHG emissions and is the second highest emitter behind the energy industry. Although on the one
    hand it has a significant impact on the global environment, it is also majorly affected by global
    environmental change. Moreover, around one-third of all food produced globally is wasted, and around
    one-third of the global population, or 2.8 billion people, do not have access to healthy food.
    As above, there is significant room for change in the agrifood system. At the Ajinomoto Group, we have
    been working on a biocycle to transform fermentation byproducts into fertilizer and feed, circulating
    nutrients to support the production of agricultural and livestock products, and improving both the global
    environment and QOL for farmers. Based on these activities, more recently we have been working on
    businesses that reduce environmental impact and promote recycling in the agricultural and livestock
    industries. Moreover, throughout our 110-year history, we have supported nutritionally balanced food
    through products and solutions, in line with global food cultures and without compromising on taste. In
    addition to the nutritional benefits of food, it has also become clear through global studies that cooking
    and eating with others is linked to subjective well-being.
    The Ajinomoto Group is engaged in a wide range of businesses based on its proprietary strength,
    “AminoScience,” including the Food Products business, which includes seasonings, processed foods, and
    frozen foods, as well as Healthcare and Electronic Materials. Moving forward, we will continue to make
    use of our tangible and intangible assets and work with scientists, policymakers, business leaders, and
    other global and local stakeholders to steadily reduce negative impacts. At the same time, we will aim to
    create more positive impacts for society throughout the value chain.
    We consider human assets to be the source of all our intangible assets and fundamental to the above
    activities. We have therefore positioned employee engagement as a key factor to improving corporate
    value. We are also reinforcing our human resource investments to ensure that our diverse personnel with
    purpose can work more closely with consumers and customers to co-create innovation.

(3) Risk management
    To achieve the Medium-Term ASV Initiatives 2030 Roadmap, we must identify risks accurately and
    respond to these risks promptly and appropriately. The Sustainability Committee and the Risk
    Management Committee work closely together to ensure no risk is left unaddressed between the two. The
    committees select and identify risks and opportunities based on important matters (Materiality) for the
    Ajinomoto Group and propose these risks and opportunities to the Executive Committee. The
    Sustainability Committee formulates response measures and manages progress on matters related to
    sustainability, including social, environmental, and nutritional issues. The Risk Management Committee
    handles risks that require management attention (e.g., pandemics, geopolitical risks, and information
    security risks).



                                                    - 23 -
     We implement risk management processes at each domestic and overseas work site to identify risks and
     formulate countermeasures, taking individual business strategies and local political, economic, and social
     conditions into account. The Risk Management Committee improves these processes and compiles the
     risks identified by each work site and addresses those that management should take the initiative to
     address. In addition, each business and corporation has formulated a business continuity plan (BCP) in
     preparation for emergencies and The Risk Management Committee has established a system for constant
     verification of each BCP’s effectiveness and manages the risk response. Full-time Audit Committee
     members attend the Sustainability Committee and the Risk Management Committee to monitor risk
     management process.


(4) Metrics and targets
     The Ajinomoto Group is currently addressing Six Material Themes (see page 21), and has set targets and
     KPIs associated with these themes not only for the reduction of negative impacts, such as environmental
     impact, but also for the creation of positive impacts across society using its proprietary strength,
     “AminoScience.”
     The Executive Committee is responsible for checking the progress and performance of the Group’s main
     initiatives.

<Our approach to climate change>
(1) Governance
      The Company’s governance for climate change issues is as described in <Our approach to sustainability>.

(2) Strategy
      The Ajinomoto Group has a wide range of product areas in the food business, from seasonings and foods
      to frozen foods, and is also expanding its business into fields such as healthcare. Climate change affects
      the Group’s business in many ways, including delays to business due to large-scale natural disasters,
      impact on procuring raw materials such as agricultural produce and fuels, and changes in product
      consumption.

      (i)     Scenario analysis assumptions
              Based on the scenarios that the average global temperature will rise from post-industrial revolution
              levels by 1.5°C or 4°C by 2100*1, in FY2024, we again conducted a scenario analysis on the impact
              of climate change between 2030 and 2050 for global umami seasonings and mainstay domestic and
              overseas products.
              Among the effects of climate change impacting production over the short, medium, and long term,
              drought, floods, rising sea levels, and changing yields of raw materials were analyzed as physical
              risks, while the introduction of carbon pricing and tightening of other laws and regulations, rising
              energy prices, and changes in consumer preferences were analyzed as transition risks.
              The tables in (ii) and (iii) show risks and opportunities, respectively, in scenario analysis when the
              average temperature difference between the 1.5°C and 4°C scenarios as of 2030 is considered to be
              about 0.2°C with no significant difference in physical risk, and when the average temperature
              difference as of 2050 is expected to be about 1°C with differences in physical risks.
              The following is a summary of the changes in the assumptions used in our scenario analysis to date.

        (iv) Reflecting scenario analysis results in strategy
            a.     Reflection in our business strategy
                   Based on the impact of the scenario analysis on our business, we plan to invest in fossil fuel
                   phase-out and the use of renewable energies, as well as eco-friendly manufacturing methods to
                   further reduce our GHG emissions in the future. We will also work on formulating new business
                   strategies to achieve ASV, where sustainability initiatives lead to greater added value for our
                   products.
                   We will review risks and opportunities in scenario analyses for FY2025 and beyond, based on
                   updated data from various sources.

            b.     Reflection on financing strategy
                   Sustainable finance forms the basis for acquiring the necessary funds for our various initiatives.
                   Beginning with the issuance of sustainable bonds in October 2021, we have continued to
                   procure funds through sustainable finance. Our efforts here include securing a commitment line
                   agreement through positive impact financing in January 2022, a commitment line agreement
                   through Sustainability Linked Loans in December 2022, and the issuance of Sustainability
                   Linked Bonds in June 2023*5. Most recently, we issued two new sustainability-linked loans in
                   March and April of 2024.
                   Through this financing, we will further accelerate our efforts to realize one of our two outcomes
                   by 2030, namely, to reduce our environmental impact by 50%, as well as to realize a sustainable
                   society.

(ii) FY2024 results
    Total Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions for FY2024 decreased by nearly 160,000 t-CO2e from the
    previous fiscal year. This reduction was driven by full transition from coal to biomass at P.T.
    AJINOMOTO INDONESIA, the complete shift from heavy oil to city gas at the Ajinomoto Co.,
    Inc. Kyushu Plant, and procurement of renewable energy certificates by P.T. AJINOMOTO
    INDONESIA.
    Scope 3 GHG emissions (covering all categories) decreased by approximately 3% year on year,
    despite an increase in production volume. This result was due to the use of more primary data on
    raw materials and improved calculation accuracy. Emissions declined by 17% compared to the base
    year of FY2018, reflecting a decrease in the Group’s total production volume (excluding
    retrospective adjustments for emissions from businesses that left the Group after the base year).




    Our reductions in Scope 1 and 2 emissions and Scope 3 emissions (excluding Category 11)
    retroactively adjusted to include emissions from companies excluded from the Ajinomoto Group
    after FY2019 in accordance with SBTi standard, in relation to the SBTi-approved Scope 1 and 2
    emissions target (-50.4% vs. FY2018) and Scope 3 emissions target (-30% vs. FY2018; excluding
    Category 11), were 43% and 13%, respectively. For Scope 1 and 2, we are on track to achieve
    approximately 90% of our target in our current plan. However, we will consider further reduction
    activities to achieve even greater emissions reductions. For Scope 3, we will continue our efforts to
    reduce GHG emissions through primary data collection and reduction initiatives enabled by deeper

           (iii) Efforts to achieve targets
                Our measures to meet our Scope 1 and 2 targets include conducting energy-saving activities,
                switching to fuels with low GHG emissions, using renewables such as biomass and solar power, and
                introducing processes to lower energy consumption (e.g., procurement of renewable energy
                certificates at Group companies in Japan).
                For Scope 3 targets, raw materials are causing approximately 60% of total GHG emissions over the
                whole product life cycle. Therefore, we encourage raw materials suppliers to reduce their GHGs and
                consider introducing new technologies and reducing GHG emissions through agricultural initiatives
                centered on regenerative agriculture.

<Our approach to biodiversity>
(1) Governance
     The Company’s governance for biodiversity is as described in <Our approach to sustainability>.

(2) Strategy
     The Ajinomoto Group offers a wide range of products in the food business, from seasonings and food
     products to frozen foods. We are also expanding into healthcare and other fields. Our businesses heavily
     depend on the bounty of nature, such as agriculture, livestock, and fishery resources, genetic resources,
     water, soil, and pollinators such as insects. These natural bounties come from healthy biodiversity shaped
     by the diversity of living organisms and their connections. However, biodiversity is currently being lost at
     an unprecedented rate, making biodiversity conservation a pressing issue worldwide. In July 2023, the
     Ajinomoto Group created the Ajinomoto Group Biodiversity Guidelines. Since issues related to
     biodiversity are also closely related to environmental boundaries and social issues such as climate change,
     water and soil, waste, and human rights, we will work to resolve these issues so as to create mutual
     benefit.

     (i)    LEAP approach
            The LEAP approach is guidance proposed by the Task Force on Nature-related Financial
            Disclosures (TNFD) that provides a process for the systematic, science-based assessment of nature-
            related risks and opportunities within corporations and financial institutions.
            In FY2023, we used the LEAP approach to assess risks and opportunities based on an analysis of
            dependencies and impacts in eligible businesses of the Ajinomoto Group. In FY2024, we conducted
            a detailed analysis of sugar cane (the Assess step), physical risk of which has a significant financial
            impacts.

           a.   Selection of target raw materials
                From among the raw materials in our businesses that provide 80% coverage of net sales, we
                selected 12 raw materials that are either listed under High Impact Commodity (HIC) or High
                Impact Commodity List (HICL) provided by SBTs for Nature, created by the Science Based
                Targets Network (SBTN), and that have a large procurement volume. For this analysis, we
                selected sugar cane, cassava, corn, raw milk, soybeans, rapeseed, rice, cattle, coffee, palm,
                copper, and crude oil. Note that we excluded paper (packaging material), which is considered an
                HICL material.

              c.      Results of detailed sugar cane analysis
                       Sugar cane was one of raw materials with the highest level of risk in the above three-step LEA
                       analysis. We therefore conducted a detailed analysis of sugar cane in Thailand, Indonesia, and
                       Brazil, where there is expected to be a significant loss of nature by 2050. Specifically, we
                       conducted a database analysis of water risk, deforestation risk, and soil degradation risk at four
                       random farming areas within sugar cane procurement zones, with a focus on all procurement
                       mills. Our analysis showed that the relatively high-risk areas (deforestation) where sugar cane
                       mills are located are Banyuwangi, Jember, Pekalongan, and Pemalang in Indonesia, and
                       Sukhothai in Thailand.

         a.   Reflection in business strategy
              In FY2025, we plan to conduct a field survey of water risk, deforestation risk, and soil
              degradation risk in sugarcane farmlands. Issues related to biodiversity based on this are also
              closely related to the environment and society, including human rights, climate change, water
              and soil, and waste, and we therefore strive to solve these issues in ways that create effective
              synergies. We will also work on formulating new business strategies to achieve ASV, where
              sustainability initiatives lead to greater added value for our products.

<Our approach to human capital>
(1) Governance
     The Ajinomoto Group employs a global human resources management system that combines position
     management and talent management, based on a common foundation to foster and recruit diverse human
     resources around the world, ensuring we put the right person in the right position. Through this system,
     we are able to visualize the pool of potential successors to important positions within the Ajinomoto
     Group. Moreover, to ensure the smooth operation of our global human resources management system and
     various measures related to improving human assets, we have established the Human Resources
     Committee, which is chaired by the CEO and consists of members of the Executive Committee, and
     which is a subordinate body to the Executive Committee. A total of 10 discussions were held in FY2024.
     In terms of building a human resources pipeline, we have created succession plans for key global
     positions for three timeframes: Ready (1–3 years), Next (within 5 years), and Future (within 8 years), in
     conjunction with the Nomination Committee. In doing so, we are forming a pool of human resources for
     next-generation leaders and strengthening strategic development and appointment.




                                                  - 35 -
(2) Human resources strategy
    The Ajinomoto Group views the further accumulation and growth of four intangible assets (technology,
    human, customer, and organization) as requisite matters in achieving the challenging ASV indicators set
    forth in our 2030 Roadmap. We are therefore strengthening our initiatives for human assets, which link
    technological and customer assets and in turn spark innovation. Our major issues in the area of human
    resources are as below. To address these issues, we are rolling out global measures under a concept of
    “connecting” in terms of the four axes of purpose, challenge, diversity, and well-being (Human resource
    investments*8: approximately ¥10 billion in FY2024; cumulative more than ¥100 billion between 2023
    and 2030). Strengthening our human assets will also build as organization assets. These assets will serve
    as a major foundation to support our technological and customer assets, thereby further strengthening all
    four intangible assets.
    *8 Investment amount, including opportunity investment

    To enhance ASV as one’s own initiative, the Ajinomoto Group has introduced an ASV management cycle
    comprising the following steps: Understanding and Sense-making; Empathy and Resonance; Execution
    and Realization; and Monitoring and Improvement. As part of our initiatives to build connections
    between our companies and their human resources with a common purpose, in FY2024 we developed 49
    ambassadors who can host My Purpose Workshops, which articulate overlaps between our companies’
    purpose and individuals’ purpose. We hosted these workshops at 85 companies and reinforced the
    “Understanding and Sense-making” step. In FY2025, to reinforce the “Execution and Realization” step,
    we will roll out global measures to transform employees’ intrinsic motivation that has been further
    enhanced through the verbalization of individuals’ purpose into behavior. Moreover, to measure the
    progress of ASV engagement, we are monitoring ASV realization process scores*9 on a global scale
    through an engagement survey (FY2024: 76%; targets: 80% in FY2025 and 85% in FY2030). In FY2024,
    although scores for questions related to “encouragement for new opportunities” and “co-creation through
    inclusion” increased, positive answers for questions related to “enhancement of productivity (approval
    process issues)” decreased to 20% (down 8% over the previous year). Specifically, there were not many
    favorable answers to “I think a large number of approvals are required before day-to-day decisions are
    made in this company.” The overall score was 76%, a similar level to the previous year. We have
    positioned the improvement of approval processes as a Group-wide management issue.




    *9 The ASV realization process is composed of nine questions in our engagement survey, linking a series of processes
       from ownership of ASV by individuals to creating results as an organization. The nine items are “empathy for our
       purpose,” “customer focus,” “ASV as one’s own initiative,” “encouragement for new opportunities,” “co-creation
       through inclusion (two questions),” “enhancement of productivity,” “innovation creation,” and “creation of social and
       economic value.”


(3) Risk management
    In risk management related to human resources, we are working to expand mid-career hiring and further
    accelerate the cultivation of DX human resources. This is not only due to external environmental changes
    such as shrinking working populations due to declining birthrates and aging populations in developed
    countries such as Japan, and the obsolescence of existing skills due to the acceleration of digitalization,
    but also to capture business transformation through further business expansion in existing fields and
    promoting efforts in our four growth areas. We also view the physical and emotional health of our
    employees as the foundation for their work, and we are working to reduce potential risks through
    improving their well-being.




                                                        - 38 -
  (4) Metrics and targets
          At the Ajinomoto Group, based on the four connecting strategies, each individual one of diverse
          employees who have empathy for Ajinomoto Group Purpose takes on challenges going beyond their
          comfort zones, that is, their accustomed environments to enhance their own capabilities of executing
          strategies. Leveraging such individual capabilities, we promote diversity (DE&I) from knowledge,
          experience, and attribute perspectives to improve our ability to take action as a team. In our efforts to
          build connections between strategies and human resources through challenges, Ajinomoto Co., Inc. has
          been working to provide further opportunities for employees to go beyond their comfort zones to take on
          challenges, such as by strengthening self-nomination transfers and introducing the TRY&A-CROSS
          framework to encourage voluntary participation in cross-organizational projects. Globally, the Ajinomoto
          Group is also promoting human resource exchanges between overseas subsidiaries. In a Group-wide
          engagement survey, a significant 89% of employees answered that they had achieved one thing that they
          thought would be a challenge for them, confirming a high level of motivation among employees to take
          on challenges. To foster a culture further conducive to trying new things, we will work to roll out
          initiatives for self-nomination on a global scale.
          In our efforts to build connections among diverse human resources across the globe, through which we
          aim to transform individual capabilities enhanced through challenges into team capabilities, the diversity
          (from perspectives of gender, nationality, and affiliation) of the Ajinomoto Group’s leadership (executive
          officers, corporate executives, and GEMs) across 128 positions steadily trended and was 25% in FY2024.
          We have created succession plans for the relevant positions using three timeframes, Ready (1–3 years),
          Next (within 5 years), and Future (within 8 years), and will continue to strengthen our initiatives moving
          forward. In terms of mid-career hires, through which we can obtain external knowledge and experiences,
          the recruitment rate of mid-career hires among all new employees joining Ajinomoto Co., Inc. in FY2024
          was 49%, a similar level to the previous year, while the number of mid-career hires increased by 122%
          year on year. However, one particular issue in Japan is the creation of a preliminary candidate group of
          female managers. At Ajinomoto Co., Inc., the ratio of female managers remained at 14%, almost
          unchanged from the previous year. To an engagement survey question, “If I receive an offer to take a
          higher position, I will accept it,” 70% of men gives a positive answer while 53% of women gives a
          positive answer, showing a difference between men and women. This, however, shows a willingness of
          more than half of female employees to take on higher positions, with the figure higher among those in
          their 20s and 30s at 65%. Meanwhile, upon investigation of the factors that are preventing women from
          advancing into managerial positions, we discovered a lack of understanding of the significance and
          purpose of DE&I initiatives and the necessity for KPIs that are in line with the conditions in each
          workplace. We will focus on these issues and ensure further support for our ambitious female employees.
          In building connections between well-being and employees, which is fundamental to our human resource
          strategies, we achieved a high well-being engagement score of 84% (average score from seven questions
          including those related to physical and emotional health, satisfaction with remuneration, and working
          environments). Aiming to ensure that working at the Ajinomoto Group naturally makes employees
          healthier, we will promote the global rollout of the Ajinomoto Group Health White Paper (A Promise to
          Health), which aims to extend the heathy life expectancy of employees and their families, and monitor
          progress through engagement surveys.

4.   Management analysis of financial position, operating results and cash flows
     Overview of results
     Upon the adoption of IFRS, the Ajinomoto Group has introduced “business profit” as a new profit level that
     will better enable investors, the Board of Directors, and the Executive Committee to grasp the core business
     results and future outlook of each business while also facilitating continual evaluation of the Group’s business
     portfolio by the Board of Directors and the Executive Committee. “Business profit” is defined as sales and
     share of profit of associates and joint ventures minus cost of sales, selling expenses, research and development
     expenses, and general and administrative expenses. Business profit does not include other operating income or
     other operating expenses.
     In addition, in the first half ended September 30, 2024, the Company finalized the provisional accounting
     treatment for a business combination and a significant revision to the initial measurement of acquisition costs
     has been made and reflected in the fiscal year ended March 31, 2024.
     Forward-looking statements in the text below are based on our assessments as of March 31, 2025.


     (1) Management’s analysis and discussion of operating results
          Aiming to maximize equity value by “deepening global financial strategy” and “reducing cost of capital”


          1. Implementing measures to generate further cash flow
          2. Switching to a global standard financial discipline indicator and appropriate cash allocation through
             the use of leverage
          3. Achieving increased equity value by improving our ROIC and optimizing the weighted average cost
             of capital (WACC)


          To achieve triple EPS, it is necessary to increase profit attributable to owners of the parent company by
          double digits in the medium to long term. In fiscal 2024, we decided on areas where we should increase
          focus and sold Ajinomoto Althea Inc. (hereinafter “Althea”) to improve profitability. Similarly, we are
          taking various measures to improve the EBITDA margin, which indicates the earning power of existing
          businesses.




                                                         - 52 -
(i)   Implementing measures to generate further cash flow
      We are strategically utilizing our growing cash flow to strengthen our financial base and improve
      capital efficiency. As an example of our global financial strategy, we hold the “Global Group CFO
      Discussion Forum” where financial officers from each region and country gather every month to
      share good examples such as cash generation and other best practices from each country and region
      and to utilize them in strategic decision-making.
      In addition to constantly evolving its business portfolio and optimizing the allocation of resources
      across the Group, the Group is also proactively working to improve the efficiency of working capital
      by, for example, promoting a program to accelerate cash generation through accounts receivable
      liquidation, introducing supplier financing in collaboration with business partners, and enhancing
      supply chain management to reduce inventory.
      Through these multifaceted initiatives, we aim to enhance cash cycle efficiency by shortening the
      cash conversion cycle and to generate further cash flows from each business, thereby steadily
      generating capital for growth investments and shareholder returns.


      <Examples of materials to discuss with financial officers of group companies>




                                              - 53 -
(ii) Switching to global standard financial discipline indicator and appropriate cash allocation through
     the use of leverage
     In order to both maintain financial soundness and maximize capital efficiency, we have changed our
     financial discipline indicator from the previous Net Debt to Equity ratio (40% to 60%) to the Net
     Debt to EBITDA ratio (<2.0x), which is also used by rating agencies and investors. This will enable
     us to monitor and adjust the appropriate debt level relative to our cash generating capacity based on
     EBITDA and will enable us to realize a flexible and agile capital management policy aimed at
     tripling EPS.
     In addition, our cash allocation policy aims to achieve a return exceeding the WACC, and the basic
     policy is to implement (1) organic growth investments, (2) M&A, etc., and (3) shareholder returns
     such as share buybacks and dividends. By appropriately utilizing leverage with an awareness of the
     rating level, we aim to maximize equity value from a long-term perspective by making investments
     that contribute to both business growth and improving our ROIC while controlling capital costs, and
     continuing to allocate funds with an emphasis on capital efficiency.


     <Approach to cash allocation>




                                              - 54 -
(iii) Achieving increased equity value by improving our ROIC and optimizing the weighted average cost
      of capital (WACC)
    We consider the reduction of the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) to be an important
    financial issue as a driver for increasing equity value, and we thoroughly implement decision-
    making with an awareness of capital cost throughout management. In light of the need for
    investment decisions based on the WACC and the need to optimize capital structure, we have
    reviewed the balance between cost of equity and cost of debt.
    Specifically, we are taking a multifaceted approach, including providing clear, investor-friendly
    disclosures, enhancing our rolling forecasts by implementing a new system, utilizing leverage in line
    with our financial structure, aiming to reduce the WACC by increasing ownership by individual
    investors, and periodically conducting our own corporate valuation and corporate valuation of the
    Ajinomoto Group to understand our current situation.
    In addition, when it comes to business investments and M&A, we are committed to concentrating
    investment in projects that are expected to produce returns exceeding the WACC. This will increase
    our ROIC/WACC spread and realize an increase in equity value over the medium to long term.
    Going forward, we will continue to evolve our financial strategies to contribute to improving the
    WACC from both a quantitative and qualitative perspective.


    <Various measures to reduce WACC>




    WACC, an important element of the Ajinomoto Group’s corporate value calculation formula,
    increased from approximately 6% to approximately 7% in fiscal 2024. The main factor was the
    increase in the risk-free rate, but we continue to work on various measures to reduce the WACC.
    One such measure is improving the accuracy of business profit forecasts by evolving rolling
    forecasts, and going forward, we will work to improve our medium- to long-term bottom-line
    management.




                                            - 55 -
    (2) Production, orders received, and sales
          The Ajinomoto Group produces and sells a broad and diverse range of products. Even for similar types of
          products, their forms and units are not necessarily the same, while some products are used in other
          segments within the Group as raw materials. Moreover, as we do not have many made-to-order products,
          we do not show the scale of production and orders received in terms of amount or quantity for each
          segment.
          As such, results for production, orders received, and sales are shown in relation to segment results in “(4)
          Analysis of operating results.”

    (3) Material accounting policies and estimates
          The Ajinomoto Group’s consolidated financial statements are prepared in accordance with the
          International Financial Reporting Standards. Details are described in “V. Financial Information, 1.
          Consolidated Financial Statements and Notes, (1) Consolidated Financial Statements.” The estimates
          required for preparation of these consolidated financial statements have been made based on reasonable
          criteria.
          The material accounting policies for preparation of the Ajinomoto Group’s consolidated financial
          statements, and accounting estimates and assumptions used in those estimates, are described under “3.
          Material Accounting Policies” and “5. Significant Accounting Judgments, Estimates, and Assumptions,”
          respectively, in “V. Financial Information, 1. Consolidated Financial Statements and Notes, (1)
          Consolidated Financial Statements, Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements.”

    (4) Analysis of operating results
          During the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, the Company’s consolidated sales increased 6.3% year on
          year, or ¥91.3 billion, to ¥1,530.5 billion. This was due to increases in sales in the Seasonings and Foods
          segment, the Frozen Foods segment, and the Healthcare and Others segment, which included the effect of
          currency translation.
          Business profit increased 7.9% year on year, or ¥11.6 billion, to ¥159.3 billion, primarily due to the effect
          of increased revenue from the Seasonings and Foods segment and the Healthcare and Others segment.
          Operating profit decreased 22.3% year on year, or ¥32.7 billion, to ¥113.9 billion mainly because
          Ajinomoto Althea’s impairment loss on goodwill and fixed assets was recorded in the current fiscal year.
          Profit attributable to owners of the parent company totaled ¥70.2 billion, down 19.3%, or ¥16.8 billion,
          due to the decrease in operating profit and other factors.

(i)   Sales
      Sales were up 6.3% or ¥91.3 billion to ¥1,530.5 billion. In Japan, sales increased 3.0% or ¥15.4
      billion to ¥525.5 billion. Overseas sales grew by 8.2% or ¥75.8 billion to ¥1,005.0 billion. In Asia,
      the Americas, and Europe, sales were up 10.6% to ¥441.8 billion, up 9.5% to ¥415.0 billion, and
      down 1.8% to ¥148.1 billion, respectively. The overseas share of sales increased to 65.7% from
      64.6% in the previous fiscal year. Note that sales are attributed to the location of sale, and are
      classified by country or region.

(ii) Cost of sales, selling expenses, research and development expenses, general and administrative
     expenses, and share of profit of associates and joint ventures
      As sales increased, the cost of sales rose by 5.6% or ¥52.0 billion to ¥979.7 billion, equivalent to
      64.0% of sales. The ratio of cost to sales improved by 0.4 percentage points year on year. Selling
      expenses increased 5.1% or ¥10.3 billion to ¥211.9 billion, mainly due to increased employee
      benefit expenses and foreign exchange effects. Research and development expenses increased 7.5%
      or ¥2.1 billion to ¥30.9 billion. General and administrative expenses increased 12.1% or ¥16.7
      billion to ¥154.8 billion, due notably to increased employee benefit expenses in connection with the
      acquisition of Forge and increased depreciation and amortization. The Group’s share of profit of
      associates and joint ventures totaled ¥6.3 billion compared to ¥4.7 billion in the previous fiscal year.

(iii) Business profit
      Business profit grew 7.9% or ¥11.6 billion to ¥159.3 billion. In Japan, business profit decreased
      1.3% to ¥60.1 billion. Overseas business profit grew by 14.3% to ¥99.1 billion. In Asia, the
      Americas, and Europe, business profit was up 10.9% to ¥75.7 billion, up 35.0% to ¥14.5 billion, and
      up 15.7% to ¥8.8 billion, respectively. The overseas share of business profit increased to 62.3%
      from 58.7% in the previous fiscal year. Note that business profit is attributed to the location of sale,
      and is classified by country or region.
      For details on business profit by segment, please see “V. Financial Information, 1. Consolidated
      Financial Statements and Notes, (1) Consolidated Financial Statements, Notes to Consolidated
      Financial Statements, 7. Segment Information.”

(iv) Other operating income and expenses
      Other operating income decreased 75.9% or ¥15.5 billion to ¥4.9 billion, mainly as a result of a
      recording of gain on sale of non-current assets in the previous fiscal year that greatly exceeded that
      of the fiscal year under review. Other operating expenses increased 134.0% or ¥28.7 billion to ¥50.2
      billion, mainly due to the recording of impairment loss on goodwill and non-current assets related to
      Althea.

(v) Operating profit
      Operating profit shrank 22.3% or ¥32.7 billion to ¥113.9 billion.

(vi) Financial income and expenses
      Financial income grew 13.1% or ¥1.0 billion to ¥8.7 billion. Financial expenses also increased
      16.2% or ¥2.0 billion to ¥14.4 billion.

   (5) Analysis of consolidated financial position as of March 31, 2025
         As of March 31, 2025, the Company’s consolidated total assets stood at ¥1,721.1 billion, a decrease of
         ¥47.2 billion from ¥1,768.3 billion at the end of the previous fiscal year on March 31, 2024. The main
         reasons for this were a decrease in assets owing to currency translation associated with the appreciation of
         the yen and a decrease in goodwill.
         Total liabilities came to ¥907.8 billion, ¥23.9 billion more than the ¥883.9 billion at the end of the
         previous fiscal year, mainly due to increases in trade and other payables as well as interest-bearing debt.
         Interest-bearing debt totaled ¥496.0 billion, an increase of ¥4.3 billion from the end of the previous fiscal
         year, due to an increase in long-term borrowings and issuance of corporate bonds.
         Total equity as of March 31, 2025, was ¥813.2 billion, ¥71.1 billion less than the ¥884.4 billion at the end
         of the previous fiscal year, mainly as a result of a decrease in equity due to the purchase of treasury stock
         and payment of dividends, which offset the increase in equity due to profit. Equity attributable to owners
         of the parent company, which is total equity minus non-controlling interests, totaled ¥746.8 billion, and
         the equity ratio attributable to owners of the parent company was 43.4%.

(7) Analysis of capital resources and liquidity
     (i)   Liquidity
           During the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, the Company ensured adequate short-term liquidity on
           hand through funding methods that mainly consisted of committed credit lines, overdraft facilities,
           and commercial paper issuance facilities.
           Moreover, in addition to maintaining an adequate ratio of liquidity on hand, the Company ensured
           funding security through committed credit lines concluded with its main banks. As of March 31,
           2025, the unused amount of committed credit lines was ¥170.0 billion in Japanese yen and US$100
           million in foreign currency. Furthermore, the Company provides an emergency loan facility to
           respond to temporary cash shortages at overseas consolidated subsidiaries with a high possibility of
           liquidity risks.

     (ii) Fund procurement
           In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, the Company raised funds through borrowings from
           financial institutions and the issuance of domestic straight bonds and commercial papers in order to
           fund its operations and to extend the maturity of short-term borrowings related to the full acquisition
           of Forge Biologics Holdings, LLC (“Forge”). In these fund procurement activities, the Company
           took into consideration the balance between direct and indirect finance from the perspective of
           funding costs and risk diversification, and the balance between long-term and short-term funding.

     (iii) Use of funds
           During the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, funds were primarily used to finance business
           operations and to extend short-term borrowings related to the full acquisition of Forge.

6. Research and development activities
   In the years leading up to 2030, we aim to become a company that contributes to the well-being of all human
   beings, our society and our planet with “AminoScience.” “AminoScience” is a collective term for the various
   materials, functions, technologies, and services derived from research and implementation processes rigorously
   focused on the functions of amino acids, since our founding. It also refers to the Ajinomoto Group’s unique
   scientific approach to connect these to resolving social issues and contributing to well-being. This is one of our
   sources of the Group’s competitive advantage, which cannot be easily imitated by other companies. Toward
   2030, we will realize the outcomes of “Reducing our environmental impact by 50%” and “Helping to
   extending the healthy life expectancy of 1 billion people” by contributing to the environment in conjunction
   with solutions to health and nutritional issues. In terms of the Ajinomoto Group growth strategies, we leverage
   “AminoScience,” the unique strength of the Ajinomoto Group, in markets with potential for medium- and long-
   term growth. Focusing on four growth areas (Healthcare, Food & Wellness, ICT, and Green) in which we can
   provide sustainable social value, we will achieve dramatic growth in the years leading to 2030 by steadily
   expanding our existing businesses and using business model transformation (BMX) to drive growth.


   During the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, research and development expenses for the Ajinomoto Group
   amounted to ¥30,921 million.
   The Ajinomoto Group holds approximately 4,200 patents in Japan and overseas.
   Below is an overview of our R&D activities in each business segment and their results during the fiscal year
   under review.


   (1) Seasonings and Foods segment
        Our R&D efforts are led by the Institute of Food Sciences and Technologies of the Company, which
        works closely with the research and development divisions of Group companies in Japan and overseas,
        including Ajinomoto AGF, Inc., Ajinomoto Frozen Foods Co., Inc., and SHANGHAI AJINOMOTO
        FOOD RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT CENTER CO., LTD. (China). Our technical development,
        product development, and application development cover every element that makes up deliciousness,
        such as taste, aroma/flavor, and texture.
        Japan has been at the forefront of developing solutions to issues such as falling birthrates, aging society,
        shrinking household size, and health consciousness. The Ajinomoto Group has been refining models to
        address these issues in Japan without compromising “Taste,” “Access (Delivering nutrition to everyone),”
        and “the Local Way of Life,” and now is extending them worldwide. Led by our global product
        development system, we use our marketing and brand strengths to continuously develop sauces,
        seasonings, and packaged food products that fit the tastes and needs of consumers in individual countries.

        Sauce & Seasonings (Japan)
        In FY2024, in the Sauce & Seasonings product category, we followed up on the strong-selling “Cook
        Do®Premium” < Spicy Mapo Tofu > with the releases of “Cook Do®Premium” < Spicy Twice-Cooked
        Pork > and “Cook Do®Premium” < Fragrant Spicy Mapo Eggplant >. These two products are part of
        “Cook Do®Premium” series that provides culinary experiences for adult palates, itself part of the Cook
        Do® series of Chinese seasonings that allow people to enjoy authentic Chinese cuisine at home. We used
        AJI-EMap®, the Ajinomoto Group’s proprietary psychological value determination technology, to
        analyze anew what consumers want from sauces and seasonings for Korean dishes and completely
        overhauled our “Cook Do®KOREA!” sauces and seasonings for Korean dishes so that consumers can
        enjoy authentic-tasting Korean dishes that fit the Japanese table. In addition to the existing products for
        < Tofu Jjigae > and < Bulgogi >, we launched two new products for < Yangnyeom Stir-fry > and < Dak
        Galbi >. In the “Cook Do® Aroma Paste” series, we released < Addictive Garlic Soy Sauce Flavor >, and
        in the “Cook Do®Today’s large plate” series, we released < Pork belly tofu > and < Pork belly and
        potatoes >.
        On our e-commerce site, we sold three varieties of Mio BrodoTM seasoning: Tomato, Cheese, and
        Seafood. Mio BrodoTM seasoning is a new kind of pasta seasoning made from two different powders, with
        the main ingredient being brodo, a basic broth used in Italian cooking. We were able to replicate the
        authentic flavor of Italy using our powdering technologies, which are also used in the Ajinomoto Group’s



                                                       - 63 -
unique Deliciousness Technology and for Knorr® Cup Soup and other products. From “BistroDo®,” we
released < Rich demiglace chicken sauté >.
From “Nabe Cube,” we released < Grilled flying fish stock >, a soy sauce-based hot pot broth with the
delicately sweet taste of grilled ago (flying fish), and updated our < Chicken broth with umami salt >,
< Rich white broth >, < Chicken broth with rich soy sauce >, < Spicy and flavorful kimchi >, and
< Supreme broth with sea bream and scallops >. From “Pasta Cube,” we released < Mellow Soy Milk
Cream >.

Sauce & Seasonings (overseas)
We are expanding our lineups of products with added value in line with the growing health consciousness
and changing lifestyles of the countries and regions in which we operate business. By using our statistical
analysis technologies to analyze the mentalities and behavior of consumers, we are further refining our
product development. In line with urbanization and changing lifestyles, there is rising demand for
products that convenient and highly processed and products with health value. AJINOMOTO
PHILIPPINES CORPORATION is implementing its BawAsin® initiative to promote salt reduction,
which is often seen as difficult to keep up for every meal without negatively affecting flavor. With the
assistance of nutritionists and culinary experts, it has developed over 100 low-salt recipes that use AJI-
NO-MOTO® umami seasoning and are tailored to local tastes, and is also conducting cooking
demonstrations of these recipes. Sazon®, which was launched by AJINOMOTO DO BRASIL
INDÚSTRIA E COMÉRCIO DE ALIMENTOS LTDA in 1988, has been widely welcomed locally for its
great taste, ease of preparation, and convenience. It now commands roughly 70% of the market, making it
one of Brazil’s top brands, used extensively in home cooking. To address the food-related issues of the
growing number of foreigners living in Japan, we have launched Sazon® (Meat, Beans, Chicken, and
Vegetables) in Japan for Brazilian residents.
We will continue to pursue deliciousness backed by the Ajinomoto Group’s unique ingredients and
technologies while reinforcing our product development in the health value area, providing delicious
flavors tailored to local tastes and contributing to health improvements.

Quick Nourishment (Japan)
In FY2024, in the Quick Nourishment segment we updated our “Knorr® Cup Soup” < Potage > to have a
richer, deeper taste by using mirepoix powder, made by slowly sautéing fragrant vegetables. From “Soup
DELI®,” we launched Creamy Carbonara, which combines our unique, chewy yet soft pasta that is easy
to restore using hot water with thick soup. In our “Knorr® Beans and vegetables to eat in potage” series,
we released Onion Gratin, with chunky beans and vegetables. We released Yum Yum® Tom Yum Kung
Noodle and Tom Yum Kung Creamy Noodle. Their distinctive features are soup packed with the true
flavor of Thailand and soft and chewy noodles, which can be easily prepared at home, simply by boiling
them.
We also launched Ajinomoto KK Protein Miso Soup, available from e-commerce sites, which makes it
easy for people to take in protein through a delicious product prepared by simply adding hot water. Each
bowl of this miso soup has 20 grams of protein, and people can take in this protein with their meals. The
protein used in this product is soy protein, which is absorbed more easily than whey protein and produces
a greater sense of satiety, and the product also has collagen for people’s beauty and health. It is made
using our unique Deliciousness Technology, so it has the bold, delicious flavor of miso soup, and our
dissolvability technologies make it easy to dissolve in hot water.

Quick Nourishment (overseas)
In our packaged food products category, we provided products that leverage the functions of amino acids
to enable people to reduce their salt intake while enjoying delicious foods and take in nutrients such as
protein, while respecting the customs and dietary preferences of the local markets in which we operate
business, as well as resources, ingredients, and stakeholders. Through this, we are working to solve health
issues related to food and lifestyles for everyone from children to adults. We will continue to pursue
deliciousness backed by the Ajinomoto Group’s unique ingredients and technologies while reinforcing
our product development in the health value area, providing delicious flavors tailored to local tastes and
contributing to health improvements.

    Coffee Products
    In the stick coffee market, from the “Chotto Zeitakuna Kohiten” brand, we launched “Chotto Zeitakuna
    Kohiten” Stick Coffee Special Blend, a stick coffee product with gentle sweetness and a milky finish that
    brings out the fragrance of the coffee, as if it had been brewed by a coffee shop master brewer. To meet
    consumer needs for products that fit their moods and their desire to enjoy a wide variety of products, we
    launched “Chotto Zeitakuna Kohiten” Regular Coffee Premium Drip Three Variety Assortment, available
    on e-commerce sites. This assortment of personal regular coffee varieties allows people to try out and
    compare the Special Blend, Mocha Blend, and Kilimanjaro Blend.
    We launched the Blendy® CAFÉLATORY® Stick series in 2023 with the theme of “a flavor that gives
    you the same satisfaction as eating sweets.” This series of products replicates the sweets that have become
    such a trend for cafés, with latte foam. The products have been well-received by people who normally do
    not buy stick products and by young people. This year, we launched three new products, Rich Pistachio
    White Chocolate Latte, Rich Melty Chocolate Latte, and Fragrant Mango & Orange Tea, and we renewed
    the popular Rich Strawberry White Chocolate Latte.
    From the Blendy® Stick series, we launched Blendy® Stick Melty Honey Black Tea au Lait, which
    combines the gentle sweetness of honey with the fragrance of black tea and the bold richness of milk. In
    the single-serving market, there is a growing need for individual portion products due to a trend for family
    members to eat different meals at home and more people choosing different products based on their mood
    and the situation. This, backed by the rise in the drinking of iced beverages at home, has created new user
    growth, which is why we launched the new flavors Fruit Tea in our Blendy® Portion series, Three Fruit
    Mixes, Matcha au Lait Base, and Apple Tea that contains apple juice from apples grown in the Tohoku
    region.

    Solutions & Ingredients
    Using unique (patent-pending) technologies developed based on our over three decades of enzyme
    research, we launched White Rice Dozo®, a revolutionary product, a first for Japan, exclusively for rice
    cookers. Simply mix it with rice and cook them together, and the enzyme action will change the structure
    of the starch in the rice to one that is harder to break down, like glutinous barley. This preserves its great
    taste but makes the sugars in the rice be absorbed more slowly.
    In restaurant and industrial-use products, from the restaurant and industrial-use Cook Do® series, we
    launched Cook Do® < Tofu & Pork Japanese-style Stir-Fry >, a low-salt (1 g/meal) product which is also
    designed for steam convection cooking and assists with daily menu preparation in senior care facilities,
    industrial catering and the like. We also launched restaurant and industrial-use Cook Do® Flavor Paste®,
    which contains a hefty 500 g of paste but comes in a spout pouch that makes it easy to hold with one hand
    and easy to squeeze out. We also renewed our restaurant and industrial-use Knorr® Quick-serve® Soup
    Potage and restaurant and industrial-use Knorr® Lunch Soup Potage, which use our unique mirepoix
    powder, created by slowly sautéing fragrant vegetables in butter, to create a quick soup with the complex
    and rich flavor and depth of vegetables simply by dissolving it in hot water.
